text: Man is a mystery: if you spend your entire life trying to puzzle it out, then do not say that you have wasted your time. I occupy myself with this mystery, because I want to be a man.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Personal correspondence (1839), as quoted in Dostoevsky: His Life and Work (1971) by Konstantin Mochulski, as translated by Michael A. Minihan, p. 17

text: I am a child of unfaith and scepticism, and shall remain so to the end of my life. How dreadfully has it tormented me, this longing for faith, which is all the stronger for the proofs I have against it. If anyone could prove to me that Christ is outside the truth, and if the truth really did exclude Christ, I should prefer to stay with Christ and not with truth.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Letter to Mme. N. D. Fonvisin (1854), as published in Letters of Fyodor Michailovitch Dostoevsky to his Family and Friends (1914), translated by Ethel Golburn Mayne, Letter XXI, p. 71

text: The principal and most basic spiritual need of the Russian People is the need for suffering, incessant and unslakeable suffering, everywhere and in everything. A current of martyrdom runs through their entire history, springing from the very heart of the People themselves. There is always an element of suffering even in their happiness, and without it their happiness is incomplete.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: The wisest of all, in my opinion, is he who can, if only once a month, call himself a fool — a faculty unheard of nowadays. They have so muddled things up that there is no telling a fool from a wise man. You don't show your own wisdom by shutting someone else in a madhouse.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: "Bobok: From Somebody's Diary" (1873), as translated by Constance Garnett in Short Stories (New York: Books, Inc, 1900)

text: All writers who have sought to represent Absolute Beauty were unequal to the task, for it is an infinitely difficult one. The beautiful is the ideal, but ideals have long been wavering. There is in the world only one figure of absolute beauty: Christ.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Letter to his Niece Sofia Alexandrovna, Geneva, January 1, 1868. Ethel Golburn Mayne, Letters of Fyodor Michailovitch Dostoyevsky to His Family and Friends (1879), Dostoevsky's Letters XXXIX, p. 136

text: The modern negationist maintains that the devil's advice is more likely to result in man's happiness than the teachings of Christ: the loaves of bread, the Tower of Babel, and the complete enslavement of the freedom of conscience. The question I should like to put to them is, in a nutshell, this: 'Do you despise or do you respect mankind, you — its future saviours?'
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Letter to Katkov, the reactionary editor of The Moscow Herald , in which The Brothers Karamazov was serialized. As quoted by David Magarshack in his 1958 translation of The Brothers Karamazov

text: I am a sick man... I am a wicked man. I am an unappealing man.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: I am a sick man... I am a wicked man. An unattractive man.

text: I did not know how to become anything; neither spiteful nor kind, neither a rascal nor an honest man, neither a hero nor an insect. An intelligent man cannot become anything seriously, and it is only the fool who becomes anything.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Once they've proved to you that a single droplet of your own fat must be dearer to you than a hundred thousand of your fellow human beings and consequently that all so-called virtues and duties are nothing but ravings and prejudices, then accept that too, because there's nothing to be done.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: What is it in us that is mellowed by civilization? All it does is to develop in man a capacity to feel a greater variety of sensations. And through this, man will yet learn how to enjoy bloodshed. Civilization has made man, if not always more bloodthirsty, at least more viciously, more horribly bloodthirsty.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: I'm a scoundrel, the nastiest, most ridiculous, pettiest, stupidest, and most envious worm of all those living on earth. All my life I have to endure insults from every louse — that's my fate.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: All is in a man's hands and he lets it all slip from cowardice. Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what they fear most.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Variant translation: "Taking a new step, uttering a new word, is what people fear most."

text: It's life that matters, nothing but life — the process of discovering, the everlasting and perpetual process, not the discovery itself, at all. There is something at the bottom of every earnest thought that springs up in any brain, which can never be communicated to others, and remains with you forever; and with it you will die, without communicating to anyone perhaps the most important of your ideas.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Though you really are mentally afflicted, the mind that matters is better in you than in any of them. For there are two sorts of mind: one that matters, and one that doesn't matter.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: There is no embarrassment in the fact that we're ridiculous. It's sometimes even good to be ridiculous, if not better: we can the sooner forgive each other, the sooner humble ourselves. To achieve perfection, one must first begin by not understanding many things! And if we understand too quickly, we may not understand well.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: I am a ridiculous person. Now they call me a madman. I do not resent it, they are all dear to me now, even when they laugh at me. Sad because they do not know the truth and I do know it. Oh, how hard it is to be the only one who knows the truth!
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: I I am a ridiculous man. They call me a madman now. That would be a distinct rise in my social position were it not that they still regard me as being as ridiculous as ever. But that does not make me angry any more. They are all dear to me now even while they laugh at me — yes, even then they are for some reason particularly dear to me. I shouldn't have minded laughing with them — not at myself, of course, but because I love them — had I not felt so sad as I looked at them. I feel sad because they do not know the truth, whereas I know it. Oh, how hard it is to be the only man to know the truth! But they won't understand that. No, they will not understand. (tr. David Magarshack , 2005
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: It seemed clear to me that life and the world somehow depended upon me now. If I shot myself the world would cease to be at least for me. As soon as my consciousness is extinguished the whole world will vanish too and become void like a phantom, for possibly all this world and all these people are only me myself.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: Dreams seem to be spurred on not by reason but by desire, not by the head but by the heart.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: Does it matter whether it was a dream or reality, if the dream made known to me the truth? If once one has recognized the truth and seen it, you know that it is the truth and that there is no other and there cannot be, whether you are asleep or awake. My dream revealed to me a different life, renewed, grand and full of power!
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I dreamt I aimed the revolver at my heart, not my head, though I had meant to fire at my temple. After a second, my world began to heave, and I pulled the trigger.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: They desired nothing and were at peace; they did not aspire to knowledge of life as we aspire to understand it, because their lives were full. Our science seeks to explain what life is, aspiring to understand it to teach others how to love, while they, without science, knew how to live.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: They seemed to do nothing but admire one another. It was like being in love with each other, but an all-embracing, universal feeling.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: How can I help believing it was all true? It was perhaps a thousand times brighter, happier, and more joyful than I describe. Granted I dreamed it, yet it must have been real. Perhaps it was not a dream at all!
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I only know that I was the cause of their sin and downfall. Like a vile trichina, like a germ of the plague, I contaminated this earth, so happy and sinless before my coming. They learnt to lie, grew fond of lying, and discovered the charm of falsehood.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I yearned for suffering, longing that my blood be drained to the last drop in these agonies. But they only laughed, declaring they had only got what they wanted, and that all that now was could not have been otherwise.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I go to spread the tidings — of the truth, for I have seen it, seen it with my own eyes, seen it in all its glory.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I have seen the truth: people can be beautiful and happy without losing the power of living on earth. I will not and cannot believe that evil is the normal condition of mankind. I have seen it in such full perfection that I cannot believe it is impossible for people to have it.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: What is a dream? And is not our life a dream? The chief thing is to love others like yourself, and that's everything. It's an old truth, told a billion times, but it has not formed part of our lives! The consciousness of life is higher than life, the knowledge of the laws of happiness is higher than happiness — that is what one must contend against.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: Men are made for happiness, and anyone who is completely happy has a right to say to himself, 'I am doing God's will on earth.' All the righteous, all the saints, all the holy martyrs were happy.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: I don't want harmony. From love for humanity I don't want it. I would rather be left with the unavenged suffering. Too high a price is asked for harmony; it's beyond our means to pay so much to enter on it. I most respectfully return him the ticket.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Book II, Chapter 4: Rebellion (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: 'I love humanity,' he said, 'but I wonder at myself. The more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular. As soon as anyone is near me, his personality disturbs my self-complacency and restricts my freedom. The more I detest men individually, the more ardent becomes my love for humanity.'
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: How many meek and humble monks yearn for solitude and fervent prayer in peace! From them, perhaps, the salvation of Russia will come. In their solitude, they keep the image of Christ fair and undefiled, ready to show it to the tottering creeds of the world.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Book VI, Chapter 3: Conversations and Exhortations of Father Zossima; The Russian Monk and his possible Significance (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Love a man even in his sin, for that is the semblance of Divine Love and is the highest love on earth. Love all God's creation. If you love everything, you will perceive the divine mystery in things, and come to love the world with an all-embracing love. Everything, like the ocean, flows and enters into contact with everything else.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Book VI, Chapter 3: Conversations and Exhortations of Father Zossima; Of Prayer, of Love, and of Contact with other Worlds (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: What is hell? I maintain that it is the suffering of being unable to love.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: A beast can never be so cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. The tiger only tears and gnaws; he would never think of nailing people by the ears.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. Active love is labour and fortitude, a complete science. Just when you see with horror that in spite of all your efforts you are getting farther from your goal, at that very moment you will reach it and behold the miraculous power of the Lord who has been all the time loving and mysteriously guiding you.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Being in love doesn't mean loving. You may be in love with a woman and yet hate her.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Why count the days, when even one day is enough for a man to know all happiness?
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: From Dostoevsky, I learned how characters are made: their inner secrets, their contradictions and complications, and how strong and helpless they are.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Dostoyevski the artist is incomparably more profound than Dostoyevski the publicist.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Nadezhda Mandelstam Hope Abandoned (1974) Translated from the Russian by Max Hayward

text: Dostoevsky, the only psychologist from whom I had something to learn.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Friedrich Nietzsche in Twilight of the Idols (1889)

text: Dostoevsky once wrote, "If God did not exist, everything would be permitted"; and that, for existentialism, is the starting point. Everything is indeed permitted, if God does not exist, and man is in consequence forlorn, for he cannot find anything to depend upon either within or outside himself. He discovers forthwith that he is without excuse. For if indeed existence precedes essence, one will never be able to explain one's action by reference to a given and specific human nature; in other words, there is no determinism-man is free, man is freedom.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Jean-Paul Sartre Existentialism and Humanism , 1948 p. 33-34

text: Major writers are usually those who have had to struggle against the odds, while writers who have had an easy start in life are usually second rate, or at least, not quite first-rate, often tinged with a certain pessimism that arises from never having achieved a certain resistance against problems.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Colin Wilson in The Books In My Life , p. 188
